title: Successful AI integration in manufacturing hinges on employees' attitudes to AI
byline: Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
excerpt: As artificial intelligence (AI) has grown more capable, industries across China are adopting AI to improve productivity and capability. One such industry is the textile and clothing industry, which has historically been very labor-intensive.
content_html:
As artificial intelligence (AI) has grown more capable, industries across China are adopting AI to improve productivity and capability. One such industry is the textile and clothing industry, which has historically been very labor-intensive.

China is the world's largest exporter of textiles and clothing, and effective integration of AI in this industry could improve product planning, production flexibility and supply chain collaboration and usher in new segments such as wearable devices and smart clothing.

So far, discussions about corporate AI adoption have largely focused on the technology itself and the needs of management. Little attention has been paid to the perspectives of the workers who actually use these systems. Research from other countries shows that digital and technical training for textile workers is crucial for effective AI integration, and even then, there are practical limits to automation.

"These findings underscore the importance of considering employees' responses to technological change when examining AI adoption in Chinese apparel manufacturing," said Eunyoung Kim, an associate professor at the Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology.

Kim and Chen Qu, a lecturer at Dalian Polytechnic University in China, sought to understand various motivational factors among Chinese textile workers and their managers that could affect AI adoption. They surveyed employees and managers working in 200 small and medium-sized apparel manufacturing units in China.

Their findings were published on Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal Fashion and Textiles.

The survey design included several unique features. First, it was created around a combined UTAUT-TOE framework, where Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) rubrics of employees' attitudes toward AI fed into the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework to understand a manufacturer's AI adoption decisions. Second, employee and manager responses from the same organization were paired to understand correlations between expectations and attitudes at both levels.

Kim found that some expected factors positively influenced decisions to adopt AI. These include the threat of competition and a firm's dynamic capability to adapt AI. Organizations in some regions of the country were also more likely to adopt AI than others. Crucially, employees' willingness to use AI also played a role in AI adoption.

Employee willingness increased if they heard positive opinions of AI from their peers, and it was also correlated with the region where the manufacturer was located. However, willingness to use AI decreased if technicians had excessively high expectations of AI-driven performance enhancements.

"This indicates that on-the-ground employees may view overly hyped AI benefits with caution or apprehension," observed Kim.

These findings hold useful insights for small and medium-sized enterprises looking to adopt AI in manufacturing, especially those working in traditionally labor-intensive industries. Successful AI adoption cannot merely be a top-down management decision based solely on technological developments or competitive pressure. "Managers should communicate the practical value of AI more effectively and provide targeted training to enhance employees' understanding, technical competence and confidence in using AI technologies," recommends Kim.

These findings will also guide policymakers on the creation of holistic digital transformation frameworks for small and medium-sized enterprises. "By aligning individual worker readiness with organizational and regional capabilities, industries can achieve a smoother, more sustainable transition to AI-driven manufacturing without alienating their workforce," concludes Kim.

More information

Chen Qu et al., Employees' behavioural intentions as a mediator of artificial intelligence adoption: a UTAUT-TOE study of Chinese small and medium-sized apparel manufacturing enterprises, Fashion and Textiles (2026). DOI: 10.1186/s40691-026-00497-4
